name: Albuterol (Salbutamol)

angle.text: Albuterol is an asthma rescue inhaler that some bodybuilders use for fat loss and muscle retention during cuts. Evidence for that use is scattered anecdote plus small lean-mass studies of oral dosing; its studied purpose is bronchospasm.

summary: The standard asthma rescue inhaler; its use for fat loss or muscle is limited to scattered bodybuilder use and small lean-mass studies of oral dosing.
note: Prescription asthma drug; beta-2 agonists are regulated in sport.
currentQuick:
Albuterol (salbutamol) is a short-acting beta-2 agonist used as a rescue bronchodilator for asthma and COPD. It is among the most prescribed medicines in the US.
Wikipedia notes that some recreational bodybuilders use albuterol and other beta-2 agonists, and that oral use has been studied for muscle wasting and obesity, with human studies reporting more lean mass and less fat mass. The sources reviewed contain no trials in healthy people seeking cosmetic changes.
How it works: It activates beta-2 adrenergic receptors, raising cAMP, which relaxes airway smooth muscle; the same receptor class is involved in lipolysis and muscle effects.
Risks and caveats: Common effects are tremor, anxiety, headache, cramps, dry mouth and palpitations; higher doses can cause tachycardia, arrhythmia and low potassium. Asthma research has examined links between heavy beta-agonist use and asthma death. It is prescription-only in the US, UK and Canada.
deepLead:
Albuterol, known as salbutamol outside the US, is a short-acting beta-2 adrenergic agonist sold as Ventolin, ProAir and Proventil, among others. It is a first-line rescue bronchodilator for bronchospasm in asthma and COPD. 
It was discovered in 1966 by a team led by David Jack at Allen & Hanburys, launched in the UK in 1969 as Ventolin and approved in the US in 1982. 
Its place in appearance discussion rests on its being a beta-2 agonist: Wikipedia reports use by some recreational bodybuilders and small studies of oral dosing for lean mass.  Published trials of its use for cosmetic fat loss or muscle in healthy people were not identified in the reviewed sources.

name: Terbutaline

angle.text: Terbutaline is a prescription asthma beta-2 agonist that physique forums group with albuterol and clenbuterol as a possible aid to leanness. It is studied for bronchospasm, and appearance trials do not exist.

summary: A prescription beta-2 agonist for asthma with an FDA boxed warning against use in preterm labour; no appearance trials exist.
note: Boxed warning: oral terbutaline not approved for tocolysis; serious maternal heart events and deaths reported.
currentQuick:
Terbutaline is a beta-2 adrenergic agonist bronchodilator used as a reliever for asthma and reversible airway disease. It is available as tablets and injection and, outside the US, as an inhaler.
It appears in appearance discussion only as a member of the beta-2 agonist family. The sources reviewed do not document its use for fat loss or muscle and contain no trials for that purpose.
How it works: It selectively stimulates beta-2 receptors, raising cAMP and relaxing bronchial smooth muscle. Wikipedia reports an elimination half-life of 11 to 16 hours and notes it is less susceptible to metabolism by COMT than catecholamines.
Risks and caveats: The label lists nervousness, tremor, headache, palpitations and tachycardia, and carries a boxed warning against use for preterm labour after maternal deaths and serious cardiac events. It is prescription-only, and WADA prohibits it except inhaled with a prior therapeutic use exemption.
deepLead:
Terbutaline is a selective beta-2 adrenergic agonist sold as Bricanyl, Brethine and Marex, among other names. It was patented in 1966, entered medical use in 1970 and is indicated for preventing and reversing bronchospasm in people aged 12 and older with asthma, bronchitis and emphysema. 
It has also been used off-label to delay preterm labour, which led the FDA in 2011 to add a boxed warning on injectable and oral forms. 
No trials of terbutaline for fat loss or muscle gain were identified in the sources reviewed, and the reviewed encyclopedic sources do not describe such use.

name: Rimonabant (Acomplia)

angle.text: Rimonabant was a prescription weight-loss pill that blocks the CB1 receptor to cut appetite, and it is discussed as a past example of pharmaceutical fat loss. Trials showed weight loss; it was withdrawn in 2008 over mood effects.

summary: A withdrawn prescription weight-loss pill that blocks the CB1 receptor; it produced weight loss in trials but was pulled in 2008 over depression and suicidality.
note: Withdrawn worldwide in 2008-2009 over psychiatric adverse events; never approved in the US.
currentQuick:
Rimonabant was an oral prescription drug for obesity that blocked the cannabinoid-1 receptor, the pathway involved in THC-driven appetite. In large trials it produced greater weight loss than placebo alongside diet and exercise.
It was approved in the EU in 2006 and rejected by the FDA in 2007. It was withdrawn from the market worldwide after psychiatric adverse events were reported.
How it works: It acts as an inverse agonist at CB1 receptors in the brain and body, which reduces the reward and appetite signaling driven by the endocannabinoid system.
Risks and caveats: Trials and post-marketing data linked it to depression, anxiety and suicidal ideation, which led the EMA to recommend suspension in October 2008. It is no longer legally marketed in the EU, Brazil or India and was never approved in the US.
deepLead:
Rimonabant, sold as Acomplia (and Zimulti), is an oral anti-obesity drug that blocks the cannabinoid-1 (CB1) receptor. It was developed by Sanofi-Aventis and was the first CB1 inverse agonist approved anywhere. 
In the large Rimonabant in Obesity (RIO) trials, people taking 20 mg a day alongside diet and exercise lost more weight than those on placebo, with improvements in waist circumference and lipid measures.  The European Commission approved it in 2006, but the US FDA did not approve it, and it was withdrawn worldwide in late 2008 after psychiatric adverse events, including depression and suicidal ideation, were reported. 
Rimonabant matters to appearance and fat-loss discussion mainly as a cautionary history of a prescription weight-loss drug. No community material about its use for cosmetic purposes was identified, so this article covers its medical record.

name: Lorcaserin (Belviq)

angle.text: Lorcaserin (Belviq) was an FDA-approved prescription weight-loss pill that curbed appetite through serotonin 5-HT2C receptors. Trials showed modest weight loss compared with placebo, and it was withdrawn in 2020 over a cancer signal.

summary: An FDA-approved prescription weight-loss pill (Belviq) that modestly outperformed placebo in trials and was pulled in 2020 over a cancer signal.
note: Withdrawn from the US market in 2020 after a trial found more cancer diagnoses on the drug.
currentQuick:
Lorcaserin was a prescription pill for chronic weight management, approved in the US in 2012. In trials it produced roughly 3 to 3.7 percent more weight loss than placebo over up to a year, with diet and exercise counseling.
In 2020 the FDA requested its withdrawal after a large cardiovascular safety trial reported more cancer diagnoses among users than on placebo.
How it works: It selectively activates serotonin 5-HT2C receptors in the hypothalamus, which is thought to increase feelings of fullness.
Risks and caveats: The main documented concern is the cancer imbalance seen in CAMELLIA-TIMI 61. Doses above the approved range have produced hallucinogenic effects, and the DEA classified it as Schedule IV. It is no longer marketed in the US.
deepLead:
Lorcaserin, sold as Belviq, is a selective serotonin 5-HT2C receptor agonist that was prescribed for chronic weight management. It was developed by Arena Pharmaceuticals and approved by the US FDA in 2012. 
In placebo-controlled trials of nearly 8,000 participants it produced an average weight loss of roughly 3 to 3.7 percent more than placebo over up to a year, alongside diet and exercise counseling.  In February 2020 the FDA asked the manufacturer to withdraw it after a large safety trial found more cancer diagnoses among people taking it than on placebo, and approval was withdrawn in September 2020. 
No community material tying lorcaserin to appearance or looksmaxxing was identified; this article describes its medical record.

name: Fenfluramine / phentermine (Fen-Phen)

angle.text: Fen-phen was a 1990s prescription pairing of two appetite suppressants, taken for weight loss and now cited as a historical diet-drug example. It produced weight loss in its era and was withdrawn in 1997 after heart valve problems.

summary: A 1990s prescription weight-loss drug pairing withdrawn in 1997 after heart valve damage and pulmonary hypertension were linked to it.
note: Fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine were withdrawn from the US market in 1997 over valvular heart disease.
currentQuick:
Fen-phen was the nickname for taking fenfluramine and phentermine together to lose weight. A 1984 trial reported greater weight loss than placebo, and use grew widely in the 1990s.
In 1997 reports of heart valve abnormalities led the FDA to request withdrawal of fenfluramine, and the episode produced tens of thousands of lawsuits.
How it works: Fenfluramine mainly releases serotonin and phentermine mainly releases norepinephrine, which together suppress appetite. The valve damage is attributed to fenfluramine's activation of 5-HT2B receptors on heart valves.
Risks and caveats: Documented harms are valvular heart disease and pulmonary hypertension. Fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine are no longer marketed for weight loss in the US.
deepLead:
Fen-phen is the informal name for the combination of the appetite suppressants fenfluramine and phentermine, which was prescribed for weight loss in the United States in the 1990s.  Fenfluramine mainly releases serotonin, while phentermine mainly releases norepinephrine. 
The combination grew popular after a 1984 trial by University of Rochester researchers reported greater weight loss than placebo.  In 1997 a Mayo Clinic report linked it to heart valve abnormalities, and the FDA requested withdrawal of fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine in September 1997.  The episode produced tens of thousands of lawsuits. 
No looksmaxxing-community material about fen-phen was identified. It is documented here as a historical weight-loss drug combination, and as the reason later serotonergic obesity drugs were screened for valve safety.

name: Dexfenfluramine (Redux)

angle.text: Dexfenfluramine (Redux) was a 1990s prescription serotonin-acting diet pill for obesity, and appears in discussions of past weight-loss drugs. It was studied for appetite and weight reduction, and was pulled in 1997 over heart-valve and lung-pressure harms.

summary: The 1990s serotonin diet pill pulled from the market in 1997 after heart-valve and lung-pressure harms.
note: Withdrawn worldwide after valvular heart disease and pulmonary hypertension reports.
currentQuick:
Dexfenfluramine (Redux) was an appetite-suppressing drug approved in the US in the mid-1990s for obesity. Trials showed weight loss with diet, and it was widely prescribed, including with phentermine as fen-phen.
It was withdrawn in September 1997 after valve disease and pulmonary hypertension were reported in users. It is not available today.
How it works: It raises serotonin signalling in the brain by releasing serotonin and blocking its reuptake, which reduces appetite. Its metabolite also activates 5-HT2B receptors, which researchers link to the heart and lung harms.
Risks and caveats: Documented harms include heart-valve disease and pulmonary hypertension, which led to withdrawal. It is not marketed anywhere reported in the sources and is not a legitimate option today.
deepLead:
Dexfenfluramine, sold in the United States under the brand name Redux, is the dextrorotatory enantiomer of fenfluramine and was developed as a serotonin-acting appetite suppressant for obesity. It is structurally related to amphetamine but is described as lacking amphetamine-type stimulant effects.
Interneuron Pharmaceuticals, co-founded by MIT researcher Richard Wurtman, developed the drug and licensed its patent to Wyeth-Ayerst Laboratories. The FDA approved it for weight loss in the mid-1990s, and approval was withdrawn in September 1997 after reports of cardiovascular harm, chiefly heart-valve disease and pulmonary hypertension.
Controlled trials from the 1980s and 1990s examined long-term dexfenfluramine treatment in obesity, and later pharmacology work linked the drug's cardiac and pulmonary harms to activation of the serotonin 5-HT2B receptor by its active metabolite. It is no longer marketed, and it appears in appearance-focused discussion mainly as a historical diet drug and as half of the "fen-phen" combination.

name: Phenylpropanolamine

angle.text: Phenylpropanolamine was a decongestant and over-the-counter diet-pill stimulant, once common in weight-loss products and cited as a historical appetite suppressant. It was removed from the market in the early 2000s after a hemorrhagic stroke link.

summary: Former OTC decongestant and diet-pill stimulant pulled in the early 2000s after a hemorrhagic stroke link.
note: Withdrawn in the US, Canada and Australia over hemorrhagic stroke risk.
currentQuick:
Phenylpropanolamine was a stimulant-like ingredient in cold remedies and diet pills such as Dexatrim and Acutrim. Some studies showed weight loss, though its evidence base for that use is modest.
A 2000 case-control study linked it to hemorrhagic stroke, and the FDA, Canada and Australia withdrew it in 2000-2005.
How it works: It releases norepinephrine from nerve endings, tightening blood vessels in the nose and, at higher doses, acting on the brain to reduce appetite. It also raises blood pressure and heart rate.
Risks and caveats: Documented harms include raised blood pressure and a rare but serious association with hemorrhagic stroke. It is withdrawn for human use in several countries and is regulated in the US as an amphetamine precursor.
deepLead:
Phenylpropanolamine (PPA) is a sympathomimetic drug related to ephedrine and amphetamine that was long used as a nasal decongestant and as an over-the-counter and prescription appetite suppressant. It was a common ingredient of cold remedies and diet aids.
It is mainly a norepinephrine-releasing agent, with weaker dopamine release. Its documented effects include raised heart rate and blood pressure, and it has been rarely linked to hemorrhagic stroke. A 2000 case-control study in the New England Journal of Medicine reported an association between PPA-containing products, including appetite suppressants, and hemorrhagic stroke, and regulators then moved to withdraw it.
In November 2000 the US FDA advised against its use, estimating 200 to 500 strokes per year among users aged 18-49, and it was removed from over-the-counter sale in the following years. Canada withdrew it in May 2001 and Australia by July 2001. It is no longer a mainstream product, though it is sometimes mentioned in weight-loss discussions as a former diet-pill ingredient.

name: Obetrol (amphetamine salts)

angle.text: Obetrol was a 1950s and 1960s prescription diet pill of amphetamine and methamphetamine salts marketed for obesity, and is cited as the ancestor of Adderall. It is of historical interest in diet-pill discussions.

summary: The 1960s amphetamine-and-methamphetamine diet pill that became Adderall's ancestor.
note: Approval withdrawn in 1973; contained amphetamine and methamphetamine salts.
currentQuick:
Obetrol was a brand-name US prescription pill from the 1950s-60s that combined amphetamine and methamphetamine salts for weight loss. It was approved in 1960 and its approval was withdrawn in 1973.
Its later methamphetamine-free reformulation became Adderall, approved for ADHD in 1996.
How it works: As a stimulant mixture, it suppressed appetite through the central nervous system effects typical of amphetamines.
Risks and caveats: Amphetamines carry misuse and cardiovascular concerns, and the 1973 withdrawal cited weak efficacy evidence as well as the speed-epidemic context. It is no longer sold.
deepLead:
Obetrol was a prescription diet pill sold in the United States in the 1950s and 1960s by Obetrol Pharmaceuticals, a division of Rexar Pharmacal. It combined four amphetamine and methamphetamine salts and was marketed for exogenous obesity.
The original 10 mg tablet reportedly held 2.5 mg each of methamphetamine saccharate, methamphetamine hydrochloride, racemic amphetamine sulfate and dextroamphetamine sulfate, with a 20 mg version doubling the amounts. The FDA approved the formula in January 1960 and withdrew approval in September 1973, citing weak supporting research.
Rexar later dropped the methamphetamine salts, and after Richwood Pharmaceuticals acquired Rexar in 1993 the reformulated product was renamed Adderall, which was approved for ADHD in February 1996. No drug marketed as Obetrol exists today.

name: Cetilistat

angle.text: Cetilistat is an orlistat-style lipase inhibitor, taken so some dietary fat passes through unabsorbed and weight comes down. It has phase 2 data for weight loss and is available mainly in Japan.

summary: An orlistat-style fat-blocking pill with phase 2 data and limited availability outside Japan.
note: Fat-blocker with orlistat-like GI side effects; not broadly approved.
currentQuick:
Cetilistat is a drug that blocks fat-digesting enzymes so some dietary fat passes out of the body. Phase 2 trials reported weight loss, with side effects similar to orlistat but possibly better tolerated.
It was developed by Alizyme, Takeda and Norgine and is reportedly approved in Japan.
How it works: It inhibits pancreatic and gastrointestinal lipases, so triglycerides are not broken down and absorbed.
Risks and caveats: Side effects are digestive (oily stools, urgency, flatulence), and fat-soluble vitamin absorption may be reduced. It is not widely available.
deepLead:
Cetilistat (ATL-962) is a pancreatic lipase inhibitor developed as an anti-obesity drug. Like orlistat, it blocks intestinal enzymes that break down dietary fat, so some ingested fat is excreted rather than absorbed.
It completed Phase 1 and 2 trials in Western countries and was developed in Japan with Takeda, which reportedly obtained approval to market it there. Takeda ended its license with Norgine in 2018.
Phase 2 trials reported weight loss in obese patients and, in people with type 2 diabetes, weight and HbA1c reductions with tolerability described as comparable to or better than orlistat. It does not have broad international availability.

name: Plenity (Gelesis100)

angle.text: Plenity is a swallowed hydrogel capsule taken before meals to promote fullness, used for weight management in adults with overweight or obesity. It is cleared as a device and trials show modest weight loss.

summary: A swallowed gel capsule that swells in the stomach to promote fullness; cleared as a device with modest evidence.
note: Device clearance, not a drug; guidelines cite limited evidence.
currentQuick:
Plenity is a capsule of cross-linked cellulose gel taken before meals with water for weight management. The FDA cleared it as a medical device in April 2019.
Reviews call its benefit modest and a 2022 AGA guideline limited its use to trials.
How it works: The gel absorbs water and swells in the stomach and small intestine, forming a semisolid mass that may promote fullness.
Risks and caveats: Side effects are mostly mild digestive symptoms. Long-term safety data beyond 24 weeks are limited, and it is contraindicated in pregnancy, malabsorption and cholestasis.
deepLead:
Plenity, developed as Gelesis100 by Gelesis, is an oral hydrogel taken in capsules before meals for weight management in adults with overweight or obesity. It is made of carboxymethylcellulose cross-linked with citric acid.
After swallowing with water, the material absorbs fluid and expands in the stomach and small intestine, forming a gel that may promote fullness and reduce calorie intake. The FDA cleared it as a medical device in April 2019 rather than as a drug.
Reviews describe adverse effects as mostly mild gastrointestinal symptoms, and note that long-term safety data beyond 24 weeks are limited. A 2022 American Gastroenterological Association guideline recommended limiting its use to clinical trials, and critics have described the benefit as small relative to side effects.

name: HU6

angle.text: HU6 is an investigational slow-release prodrug of DNP, a fat-burning mitochondrial uncoupler, and is followed by people interested in a more controlled version of DNP-style fat loss. It is in phase 2 trials and is not available as a product.

summary: An experimental, slow-release prodrug of the toxic fat-burner DNP, still in phase 2 trials.
note: Unapproved; DNP itself is associated with fatal overdoses.
currentQuick:
HU6 is an experimental pill from Rivus Pharmaceuticals designed to deliver DNP, a historic weight-loss uncoupler, in a more controlled way. It is in phase 2 trials for fatty liver, obesity and heart failure.
A 2023 phase 2a trial of 80 people reported reduced liver fat versus placebo over 61 days.
How it works: After being converted to DNP in the liver, it lets mitochondria lose energy as heat instead of making ATP.
Risks and caveats: Flushing, diarrhoea and palpitations were most common in the trial. It is unapproved, and DNP itself has caused fatal overdoses and is banned for human consumption.
deepLead:
HU6 is an investigational once-daily oral drug from Rivus Pharmaceuticals. It is a prodrug of 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP), a mitochondrial uncoupler, and is designed to give more stable blood concentrations than DNP itself.
DNP was used for weight loss in the 1930s but was judged too toxic for human consumption and is associated with fatal overdoses, so HU6 is being developed as a controlled alternative. It has been tested in phase 1 and phase 2 trials in obesity-related liver disease, overweight and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.
The main published trial is a 2023 phase 2a study in people with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and high BMI, which reported reductions in liver fat versus placebo. It is not approved anywhere and is not sold as a product.

name: UBT251

angle.text: UBT251 is an investigational once-weekly triple agonist, licensed to Novo Nordisk, that people follow as a next-generation weight-loss peptide after semaglutide and tirzepatide. Phase 2 data exist, and it is not an approved or prescribable drug.

summary: Investigational once-weekly GLP-1/GIP/glucagon triple agonist from China, licensed to Novo Nordisk; phase 2 data exist, but it is not an approved or prescribable drug.
note: Investigational only; not approved anywhere. Published human data are early-phase.
currentQuick:
UBT251 is an experimental injectable peptide that activates the GLP-1, GIP and glucagon receptors. It is being tested for obesity, type 2 diabetes, kidney disease, sleep apnea and fatty liver disease.
Two 24-week phase 2 trials in China were published in 2026, and phase 3 studies are registered. It is not approved for any use.
How it works: As a triple agonist, it is designed to combine appetite and insulin effects of GLP-1 and GIP with the energy-expenditure effects associated with glucagon-receptor activation.
Risks and caveats: Safety data are limited to early trials. The wider drug class is associated with gastrointestinal side effects. It is available only inside clinical trials.
deepLead:
UBT251 is an investigational long-acting peptide that activates three receptors at once: the glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) and glucagon receptors. It was developed by United Biotechnology, a subsidiary of The United Laboratories International Holdings (TUL) in China, and is given as a once-weekly subcutaneous injection in trials. 
It is being studied for obesity, type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease, obstructive sleep apnea and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH). In March 2025, TUL announced an exclusive licensing deal with Novo Nordisk covering development and commercialisation outside China. 
UBT251 is not an approved medicine in any jurisdiction. Published human evidence comes from a first-in-human phase 1a/1b study and two 24-week phase 2 trials in China, reported in 2026.  It belongs to the same broad class of incretin-based weight-loss peptides that includes semaglutide and tirzepatide, which are discussed in appearance and fat-loss communities, but no community discussion of UBT251 itself is documented here.

name: Benzphetamine

angle.text: Benzphetamine is a prescription amphetamine-type appetite suppressant labelled for a few weeks of obesity treatment, and appears in discussions of older weight-loss drugs. It is a Schedule III medication aimed at weight reduction, not a cosmetic drug.

summary: Old-school prescription amphetamine-type appetite suppressant labelled for a few weeks of use in obesity; Schedule III and not a cosmetic drug.
note: Controlled substance; label warns of pulmonary hypertension risk with use beyond three months.
currentQuick:
Benzphetamine is a prescription appetite suppressant related to amphetamine. In the US it is approved only for short-term use alongside a reduced-calorie diet in people with obesity.
It is a controlled substance and is not approved for cosmetic weight loss.
How it works: It is thought to increase norepinephrine and dopamine release in the brain's feeding centers, reducing appetite, and is converted in the body to amphetamine-type metabolites.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include raised heart rate and blood pressure, insomnia and restlessness. The label cites an association between long-term anorectic use and pulmonary hypertension and contraindicates use in pregnancy. It is Schedule III in the US.
deepLead:
Benzphetamine (brand name Didrex, among others) is a prescription sympathomimetic amine used as an appetite suppressant. In the United States it is labelled as a short-term adjunct, lasting a few weeks, to a calorie-restricted weight-reduction regimen for people with a body mass index of 30 kg/m2 or higher who have not responded to diet and exercise alone. 
It is related to amphetamines and is described as a prodrug that the body converts to amphetamine and methamphetamine.  It is a controlled substance, listed in Schedule III in the US. 
Its relevance to appearance culture is as one of the older prescription anorectics used for fat loss. The US label states the drug is not for long-term use, and no published community material about it is catalogued here.

name: Phendimetrazine

angle.text: Phendimetrazine is an older prescription stimulant appetite suppressant labelled for a few weeks of obesity treatment, and is mentioned alongside similar diet drugs. It is a controlled medication for weight reduction, not a cosmetic drug.

summary: Older prescription stimulant appetite suppressant, a phenmetrazine prodrug, labelled for a few weeks of obesity treatment; controlled and not a cosmetic drug.

currentQuick:
Phendimetrazine is a prescription stimulant that suppresses appetite. In the US it is labelled for short-term use with a reduced-calorie diet in people with obesity.
It is an older drug with limited modern trial data and is a controlled substance.
How it works: It is partly converted in the body to phenmetrazine, which releases norepinephrine and dopamine and reduces appetite.
Risks and caveats: The label lists raised heart rate and blood pressure, insomnia, agitation and other stimulant effects, and cites a link between long-term anorectic use and pulmonary hypertension. Safe use in pregnancy is not established. Schedule III in the US.
deepLead:
Phendimetrazine (brand names include Bontril) is a prescription stimulant of the morpholine class used as an appetite suppressant. The US label indicates it as a short-term adjunct, lasting a few weeks, to a calorie-restricted regimen in patients with a body mass index of 30 kg/m2 or higher who have not responded to diet or exercise alone. 
It acts largely as a prodrug: Wikipedia states roughly 30% of an oral dose is converted to phenmetrazine, a norepinephrine-dopamine releasing agent.  It is a Schedule III controlled substance in the US. 
Published clinical evidence for obesity is older and sparse; a narrative review lists phendimetrazine among noradrenergic drugs approved only for short-term use.  Its place in appearance culture is as one of several older prescription anorectics; no community material about it is catalogued here.

name: Diethylpropion

angle.text: Diethylpropion is an older prescription appetite suppressant labelled for a few weeks of obesity treatment, and it is discussed with other diet drugs. It is Schedule IV in the US, and the EU has recommended its withdrawal.

summary: Older prescription appetite suppressant labelled for a few weeks of obesity treatment; Schedule IV in the US and recommended for withdrawal in the EU.

currentQuick:
Diethylpropion is a prescription stimulant that reduces appetite. In the US it is labelled for a few weeks of use alongside dieting in people with obesity.
It is an older drug, included in some meta-analyses of obesity medications, and is not approved for cosmetic use.
How it works: It is converted to ethcathinone, which mainly affects norepinephrine signalling and reduces appetite.
Risks and caveats: The label lists raised heart rate and blood pressure, arrhythmia, and rare pulmonary hypertension, with a cited association for anorectic use beyond three months. It is Schedule IV in the US, and in 2022 an EMA committee recommended withdrawing it from the EU market.
deepLead:
Diethylpropion, also called amfepramone, is a prescription appetite suppressant of the phenethylamine and cathinone families. The US label indicates it as a short-term adjunct, lasting a few weeks, to a calorie-restricted regimen for people with a body mass index of 30 kg/m2 or higher who have not responded to diet or exercise alone. 
It is a prodrug of ethcathinone and is a Schedule IV controlled substance in the US.  In June 2022 the European Medicines Agency's safety committee recommended withdrawing marketing authorisations for amfepramone medicines, according to Wikipedia. 
Meta-analyses of weight-loss drugs have included diethylpropion alongside phentermine and sibutramine.  No community material about it is catalogued here.

name: Pioglitazone

angle.text: Pioglitazone is a type 2 diabetes drug known to raise subcutaneous fat, which is why appearance discussions bring it up in connection with body-fat distribution. Appearance-related claims about it are untested in humans.

summary: Prescription diabetes drug that raises subcutaneous fat; appearance-related claims about it are untested in humans.
note: Boxed warning for congestive heart failure; no cosmetic use is approved or studied.
currentQuick:
Pioglitazone is a prescription pill for type 2 diabetes that improves insulin sensitivity. It has been generic for years.
It shows up in appearance discussion through claims about fat tissue, but no human study has tested it for cosmetic purposes.
How it works: It activates PPAR-gamma receptors, mainly in fat tissue, muscle and liver, which lowers insulin resistance. Weight gain from added subcutaneous fat is a recognised effect.
Risks and caveats: The label has a boxed warning for congestive heart failure and lists edema and fractures. Bladder cancer warnings were added in 2011. It is prescription only.
deepLead:
Pioglitazone (brand name Actos) is an oral type 2 diabetes drug in the thiazolidinedione class. It was developed by Takeda, came into medical use in 1999 and is now generic. 
It activates the PPAR-gamma receptor, which is found in fat, muscle and liver tissue, and reduces insulin resistance.  Its label carries a boxed warning for congestive heart failure, and a known effect is weight gain attributed to increased subcutaneous fat. 
Pioglitazone appears in appearance-related discussion because of claims about fat tissue and, in one forum context, topical under-eye use. No published human study has tested pioglitazone for cosmetic purposes.

name: Anamorelin

angle.text: Anamorelin is an investigational oral ghrelin-receptor drug studied for cancer cachexia, and muscle-focused users follow it because it raised lean mass in trials. Those trials were in cancer patients, and appearance-use data are absent.

summary: Oral ghrelin-receptor drug studied for cancer cachexia; it raised lean mass in trials but has no appearance-use data.
note: Studied only in cancer patients; not authorised in the EU; on the WADA prohibited list.
currentQuick:
Anamorelin is an experimental oral drug that mimics ghrelin, the hunger hormone. It was developed to treat the appetite and muscle loss that come with advanced cancer.
Phase 3 trials reported gains in lean body mass without clear gains in grip strength, and European regulators declined to authorise it in 2017. A Japanese approval for cachexia has been reported. No trial has tested it for cosmetic or physique goals.
How it works: It activates the ghrelin receptor in the brain and pituitary, increasing appetite and prompting growth hormone and IGF-1 release.
Risks and caveats: Safety data come from cancer-patient trials, and EU regulators cited inadequate safety recording. It is a prescription-only, non-marketed drug in most countries and appears on the WADA prohibited list.
deepLead:
Anamorelin is an investigational oral drug that activates the ghrelin receptor (also called the growth hormone secretagogue receptor). It has been developed for cancer cachexia, the wasting syndrome of appetite loss, weight loss and muscle loss seen in advanced cancer. It also goes by the development codes ONO-7643 and RC-1291.
Its clinical research is almost entirely in cancer patients. Phase 3 trials in non-small-cell lung cancer (ROMANA 1 and 2) reported gains in lean body mass but no clear improvement in handgrip strength, and the European Medicines Agency declined marketing authorisation in 2017. A regulatory review reports that the drug was approved in Japan for cachexia in several cancer types.
No published trial has tested anamorelin for cosmetic, bodybuilding or aesthetic purposes. It is discussed in appearance-related contexts mainly as one of several ghrelin-mimetic growth hormone secretagogues. It is listed among substances prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency.

name: Macimorelin

angle.text: Macimorelin is an oral ghrelin-receptor agonist that releases growth hormone, and GH-minded users note it as a secretagogue. It is approved only as a one-time diagnostic test for adult GH deficiency, with no data on appearance.

note: Approved only as a diagnostic test; label warns of QT prolongation.
currentQuick:
Macimorelin is a prescription drug sold as Macrilen. Doctors give it once, by mouth, to see whether the pituitary releases enough growth hormone, which helps diagnose adult growth hormone deficiency.
It was approved in the US in December 2017. It is not approved as a treatment and no study has tested it for appearance.
How it works: It binds the ghrelin (GH secretagogue) receptor in the pituitary and hypothalamus, which prompts a pulse of growth hormone that can be measured.
Risks and caveats: The label lists altered taste, dizziness, headache and nausea as common reactions and warns of QT prolongation. Strong CYP3A4 inducers can distort test results.
deepLead:
Macimorelin (brand name Macrilen) is an orally active ghrelin-receptor agonist that stimulates release of growth hormone. It is approved by the US FDA as a diagnostic test for adult growth hormone deficiency (AGHD), not as a treatment.
In the test, a single oral dose is given and growth hormone levels are measured afterwards. Trials compared it with the insulin tolerance test and with arginine plus GHRH testing. The US label lists QT prolongation among its warnings.
No studies have tested macimorelin for appearance or muscle-building purposes. It appears in looksmaxxing-adjacent discussion only as one of the ghrelin-mimetic growth hormone secretagogues.

name: Capromorelin

angle.text: Capromorelin is an oral ghrelin agonist sold as a pet appetite stimulant, and it draws interest as a growth hormone secretagogue. A human older-adult trial showed a modest lean-mass change and was not pursued.

summary: Oral ghrelin agonist sold as a pet appetite stimulant; a human older-adult trial showed modest lean mass change and was not pursued.
note: Veterinary product; not approved for humans.
currentQuick:
Capromorelin is a Pfizer-developed drug that mimics ghrelin. It is sold for pets as Entyce (dogs) and Elura (cats with kidney disease).
In people, a trial in older adults reported a small lean-mass gain, but development in humans was discontinued. No study has tested it for appearance.
How it works: It activates the ghrelin/GH secretagogue receptor, raising appetite and growth hormone and IGF-1 levels.
Risks and caveats: It is a veterinary prescription drug, with vomiting and diarrhoea noted in animals. Human safety data are limited to early-phase and older-adult trials.
deepLead:
Capromorelin is an orally active ghrelin-receptor agonist and growth hormone secretagogue developed by Pfizer. It is approved for veterinary use, as Entyce for appetite stimulation in dogs (US, 2016) and Elura for weight loss in cats with chronic kidney disease (US, 2020).
Before its veterinary approvals it was studied in humans. A trial in older adults with mild functional limitation tested its effects on hormones, body composition and physical performance. Wikipedia reports that human development was discontinued, as results were not judged strong enough to continue.
No studies have examined capromorelin for cosmetic purposes in healthy people.

name: Relamorelin

angle.text: Relamorelin is an injected ghrelin analogue studied for diabetic gastroparesis, and some people group it with ghrelin-pathway muscle and appetite compounds. Phase 3 trials were terminated and appearance data do not exist.

summary: Injected ghrelin analogue tested for diabetic gastroparesis; phase 3 trials were terminated and there is no appearance data.
note: Investigational; phase 3 trials terminated.
currentQuick:
Relamorelin is an investigational injected ghrelin analogue. It was developed to speed stomach emptying in people with diabetic gastroparesis.
Phase 2 trials reported benefit on vomiting and emptying, but the phase 3 programme was terminated. It has not been tested for appearance.
How it works: It is a pentapeptide that activates the ghrelin receptor, which also raises growth hormone and appetite.
Risks and caveats: It is not approved anywhere. Safety data come from clinical trials in gastrointestinal and eating-disorder patients.
deepLead:
Relamorelin (RM-131) is a synthetic pentapeptide ghrelin analogue that is injected subcutaneously. It was developed to treat diabetic gastroparesis, a condition of delayed stomach emptying, and was also studied in constipation and anorexia nervosa.
Its phase 2 trials reported faster gastric emptying and reduced vomiting in diabetic gastroparesis. Several phase 3 trials were registered in 2017-2018 and all were later terminated. Wikipedia describes its development status as uncertain.
No studies have tested relamorelin for appearance or muscle-building purposes.
